runs.analysis: Both candidates have the right structure: a UUID id, a project_title and a final_deliverable, each within the 1-3 word limit. Both identify the Gibraltar link between Spain and Morocco. A's title, "Gibraltar Subsea Tunnel", is more descriptive than B's "Gibraltar Tunnel", which is plain and could describe any Gibraltar tunnel. A's deliverable, "Operational Transoceanic Tunnel", reuses the prompt's own wording ("transoceanic") and states the end state. Strictly, the Strait of Gibraltar is not an ocean crossing, but the prompt uses that term. B's deliverable, "Operational Submerged Tunnel", is accurate to the floating, submerged design concept. A's title and deliverable together carry more information (subsea plus transoceanic), while B's wording is slightly closer to the design. The difference is small, and I give A a slight edge for the more informative, prompt-aligned title.

Both candidates follow the schema, with 1-3 word fields and a UUID. A's deliverable, "Operational Submerged Tunnel", matches the plan's distinctive floating submerged-tunnel concept. B uses "Subsea", which can suggest a bored seabed tunnel, and "Transoceanic", which echoes the prompt but is geographically off for the Strait of Gibraltar. B's title and deliverable also overlap more. Neither mentions rail. A is slightly more precise.

Both candidates match the schema (project_title, final_deliverable, id). A's title, "Hauts-de-France Buildout", is vague. It could imply the full 9 GW buildout and doesn't say it is an AI campus. Its deliverable, "Phase 1 Operational", is 3 words but doesn't name the thing delivered. B's title, "Hauts-de-France AI Campus", is specific and descriptive. Its deliverable, "Operational Phase 1 Campus", is clearer, but it is 4 tokens and slightly exceeds the 1-3 word limit if "1" counts as a word. Neither captures the red-team, go/no-go feasibility framing. B is more informative for downstream stages, while A follows the word limit more strictly. B is slightly better overall.

Both candidates are valid, schema-conforming WBS Level 1 outputs and both pick Phase 1 as the final deliverable, which suits a skeptical, gated plan. A's title, "Hauts-de-France AI Campus", names the location and the nature of the project. B's title, "Hauts-de-France Buildout", is vague and could describe any construction project in the region. A's deliverable, "Operational Phase 1 Campus", states what is delivered. B's deliverable, "Phase 1 Operational", is terser and doesn't say what is operational. Both fit the 1-3 word limit if "Hauts-de-France" counts as one word. A is more informative and more useful to downstream stages.

Both candidates follow the schema (1-3 word title and deliverable, with an id). B's title, "Cross-Border Rail Ticketing", is slightly better because it names the cross-border scope. A's deliverable, "Interoperable European Ticketing", is more concrete and plan-specific, since it reflects OSDM interoperability and the European scope. B's "Seamless Single Ticketing" is vaguer and marketing-like. A's deliverable is more useful for downstream WBS stages, which gives A a small edge overall.

Both candidates are valid WBS Level 1 outputs. A's title ("Cross-Border Rail Ticketing") keeps the cross-border focus but may count as 4 words if the hyphen is split. Its deliverable ("Seamless Single Ticketing") is vague and describes a quality more than an end product. B's title ("Rail Through-Ticketing") is 2-3 words under either counting and uses the program's core concept, though it drops "cross-border" and "European". B's deliverable ("Interoperable European Ticketing") is more specific, restores the European scope, and matches the OSDM/interoperability goals. B's two fields are complementary, while A's repeat "ticketing". B is slightly better on word-limit compliance and deliverable quality, and A is slightly better on title scope.

Both candidates use the same title, "Leipzig Heat Response". Leipzig is a plausible non-capital EU city of about 600k, which is above the 150k–400k range in the prompt. That flaw is shared, so it doesn't separate them. Both final deliverables are three words and fit the schema. The difference is in the final deliverable. A's "Reduced Heat Impact" states an outcome or goal, not something delivered. The plan can't guarantee it, and it can't be a WBS root deliverable. B's "Operational heat response" names a working capability: the operating heat response program. The plan's end-of-month-12 deliverables include a repeatable Playbook and a functioning response system. B therefore fits better, although it largely repeats the title and isn't as concrete as "Heat Response Playbook". B's casing is slightly inconsistent with the title, but that is trivial. B is a bit better.

The two candidates share the same project title, "Leipzig Heat Response". Leipzig is a plausible non-capital EU city of the right size, so both are equally faithful there. Both are also within the 1–3 word limit. The only difference is the final deliverable. A, "Operational heat response", describes a deliverable, namely a functioning, executable response program. That fits the plan's emphasis on a municipality being able to "execute immediately". It largely repeats the title and does not name the concrete end-of-month-12 outputs: the Heat Response Playbook, cost model, evaluation report and Year-2 roadmap. B, "Reduced Heat Impact", states the goal or outcome, not something the project hands over. The plan itself says outcomes can only be shown with caveats, such as attribution of mortality. It is also vaguer, though it does capture the aim of cutting harm. Neither names the Playbook, which would have been the best choice. A is a little closer to a tangible deliverable and to what the pipeline's "final deliverable" field is meant to capture. B reads more like an objective. The margin is slim.
